terms.payload: The data a message carries: the body of a request or an event. In a DataWeave script it is called payload.
terms.JSON: A common way to write data as text: objects in { }, lists in [ ], text in quotes, numbers and true/false as they are.
terms.field: A named value inside an object, like "city": "Milan". The name is the key, the part after the colon is the value.
terms.mapping: The rules that turn data in one shape into the same data in another shape.
terms.source: The data you start from. Here, the shop's order.
terms.target: The shape you need to produce. Here, what the warehouse expects.
terms.DataWeave: The language MuleSoft uses to write mappings. It runs inside Mule apps.
terms.Mule app: An integration built with MuleSoft: it receives messages, works on them, and sends them on.
terms.selector: A dot followed by a field name, like .city. It picks that field out of the data.
terms.null: DataWeave's word for "nothing here". A missing field gives null.
terms.map: Runs the same small piece of script once for every item in a list, and collects the results into a new list.
terms.XML: Another way to write data as text, with tags like <city>Milan</city>. Common in older and enterprise systems.
terms.CSV: Comma-separated values: a table written as text, one row per line. What spreadsheets export.
terms.attributes: Details that come with a request but are not its body: headers, query parameters, the method.
terms.vars: Values a Mule app saved earlier in the same flow, so later steps can read them.
terms.webhook: A message one system sends another, on its own, to say that something just happened.
terms.property: A setting kept outside the script, in a config file, so it can differ between test and production.

body.p: Your company runs many apps: an online shop, a warehouse system, a billing tool. They don't share a brain. When the shop takes an order, it has to *tell* the warehouse, and it does that by sending a message.
The useful part of a message is its *payload*: the data itself. On the right is the payload the shop sends for one order.
It is written in *JSON*, the most common way to write data as text. Four things to know:

list: `{ }` holds an object: a set of named values. Each one is a *field*: a name in quotes, a colon, then the value.
`[ ]` holds a list. `lines` is a list of three items, one per product.
Text is in quotes, like `"Milan"`. Numbers are not, like `159`.
Values can hold more values. `customer` is an object with an `address` inside it.

body.p: To find something, follow the names from the outside in: the order, then `customer`, then `address`, then `city`.

interactive.label: Click any value in the order. The path to it lights up.

options.why: The order has no city of its own. Look inside the customer.
Right. Follow the names from the outside in.
`lines` holds the products, not where they go.

body.p: The warehouse needs the same order, but it was built by a different team, years ago, and it wants the data in its own shape.

Compare the two. The shop calls the order number `orderId`; the warehouse calls it `ref`. The shop splits the name in two; the warehouse wants one `name`. The warehouse doesn't care about prices or the email at all.
Turning one shape into the other is called *mapping*. You start from the *source* (the shop's order) and build the *target* (what the warehouse wants). Every mapping is made of a few kinds of rule:

list: **Move:** `city` sits inside `customer.address` in the source, and inside `shipTo` in the target.

body.p: Most integration work is exactly this, over and over. Before writing any code, try it by hand.

interactive.label: Click each target field to see which source fields fill it.

check.question: The warehouse's `name` needs two source fields joined. Which two?

options.why: The email is left out of the target completely.

body.p: *DataWeave* is the language MuleSoft uses to write mapping rules. It runs inside a *Mule app*: the integration that sits between the shop and the warehouse.
The step in the middle is where your script runs. Every message that passes through gets the same rules applied.
On the right is the whole mapping from the last lesson, written as a script. It has three parts:

list: **The header**, above the line: `%dw 2.0` says which DataWeave version, and `output application/json` says the result should be JSON.
**The body**, below it: a picture of the result you want, with the values filled in from `payload`.

body.p: You don't need to understand every line yet. The next three lessons take it apart piece by piece. For now, edit something in the body, say change `"ref"` to `"orderNumber"`, and watch the output follow.

check.question: Which part of the script decides that the result is JSON?

options.why: That line says which version of DataWeave the script is written in.
Right. Change it to `application/xml` and the same data comes out as XML (lesson 0.7).
The dashes only separate the header from the body.

body.p: In a script, the incoming data is always called `payload`. To point at something inside it, write a dot and the field's name: a *selector*.
`payload.customer` is the whole customer object. Keep adding dots to go deeper: `payload.customer.address.city` is `"Milan"`.
A selector on a list reaches into every item at once: `payload.lines.sku` gives the three SKUs as a list.

body.callout: A missing field is not an error
body.text: This order has no `discount`. Asking for `payload.discount` gives *null*, DataWeave's word for "nothing here". When you want a fallback instead, add `default`: `payload.discount default 0` gives `0`.

body.p: A field name with a dash or a space goes in quotes after the dot, like `payload."order-id"`.

examples.label: Into every item of a list

hints: The total sits at the top level of the order, next to `orderId`.
One dot is enough: `payload.` and the field's name.

body.p: The body of a script is a picture of the result. To build an object, write `{ }` and list its fields as `name: value`, separated by commas.
The name on the left is whatever the target wants. The value on the right can be a selector, so renaming is just this: `ref: payload.orderId`.
A value can also be fixed text in quotes, like `source: "web-shop"`, the same on every message.
To join text, use `++`. `payload.customer.firstName ++ " " ++ payload.customer.lastName` gives `"Maria Rossi"`; the `" "` in the middle is the space between the two names.
Numbers work with `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`, as on a calculator: `payload.total * 2` is `318`.
Objects can hold objects. Build `shipTo` by nesting another `{ }` inside, exactly as in the target.

examples.label: Rename and add a fixed value
An object inside an object

check.prompt: Build the warehouse's order header: `{ ref, customerName, country }`, where `customerName` is the first and last name with a space between them.
check.solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  ref: payload.orderId,
  customerName: payload.customer.firstName ++ " " ++ payload.customer.lastName,
  country: payload.customer.address.country
}
hints: Add two more `name: value` lines, separated by commas.

lessons.title: Lists: doing it for every item

body.p: An order has a list of lines, and the warehouse wants a list of items. You don't write a rule per line, since the next order might have one line or fifty. You describe what to do with *one* line, and `map` does it for every line.

Read it as: "take `payload.lines`, and for each `line`, build this". `line` is a name you choose for the current item; inside the braces, `line.sku` is that item's SKU. The result is a new list with one entry per line.
There is a short form. Without the `(line) ->` part, the current item is called `$`: `payload.lines map { sku: $.sku }`. Both mean the same. The long form reads better while you are learning.

body.text: If an order has no lines, `map` gives an empty list, `[]`. Nothing breaks.

examples.label: A picking list
examples.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload.lines map (line) -> {
  sku: line.sku,
  quantity: line.qty
}

examples.label: Working something out per item
examples.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload.lines map (line) -> {
  sku: line.sku,
  lineTotal: line.qty * line.price
}

examples.label: No lines at all

check.prompt: Return the picking list: one `{ sku, quantity, product }` per line, where `product` is the line's `name`.
check.solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
payload.lines map (line) -> {
  sku: line.sku,
  quantity: line.qty,
  product: line.name
}
hints: Inside the braces, three fields: `sku: line.sku`, then `quantity` and `product` the same way.

body.p: JSON is not the only way to write data down. Older and enterprise systems often use *XML*, with tags around each value. Spreadsheets and file drops use *CSV*: a table, one row per line, values separated by commas.
DataWeave reads all of them into the same thing, so the body of your script hardly changes. What changes is one line in the header: `output application/xml` or `output application/csv`.
Two rules come with the formats:

list: **XML needs exactly one outer element**, called the root. Wrap your result in one: `{ order: { ... } }`.
**CSV is a table**, so its result must be a list of flat objects: one object per row, one field per column.

body.p: It works the other way too. When the *input* is XML, select into it with the tag names, root first: for `<order><ref>SO-1001</ref></order>`, the value is `payload.order.ref`.

examples.label: The header as XML
The picking list as CSV
examples.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/csv
---
payload.lines map (line) -> {
  sku: line.sku,
  quantity: line.qty
}

examples.label: XML without a single root fails
examples.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/xml
---
{
  ref: payload.orderId,
  city: payload.customer.address.city

lessons.title: Where data comes from in Mule

body.p: In a real Mule app, a script can read more than the payload. Three things come up all the time:

list: `attributes`: details that arrive with a request but are not its body, such as headers and query parameters. `attributes.headers."x-source"` reads a header called x-source.
`vars`: values the Mule app saved earlier in the same flow. If an earlier step stored a correlation id, `vars.correlationId` reads it.
`p('name')`: a *property*, a setting kept in a config file instead of the script, so test and production can use different values. `p('warehouse.code')` reads it.

body.p: In DataWeave Studio, all three live in the **Context** panel under the payload: Request for attributes, Vars for vars, and Config for properties. Set them there and your script sees them exactly as it would inside Mule.

body.text: The online Playground only has the payload. Anything that reads a header, a var or a property is where DataWeave Studio earns its keep.

examples.label: A value saved earlier in the flow
A property from the Config tab
examples.script:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  ref: payload.orderId,
  warehouse: p('warehouse.code')
}

interactive.label: Change the x-source header in the Context panel and run again.

check.prompt: Return `{ ref, channel }`, where `channel` comes from the request's `x-source` header.
check.solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  ref: payload.orderId,
  channel: attributes.headers."x-source"
}
hints: The name has a dash, so it goes in quotes: `."x-source"`.

body.p: Time to put it together on a message you haven't seen. When a customer pays, the payment provider sends the shop a *webhook*: a message announcing that something happened. Here is one.
The shop wants it in this shape:

body.shape:
{
  orderId,   // the order the payment is for
  paidBy,    // the payer's name
  amount,    // in euros: the webhook sends cents, so divide by 100
  method,    // how they paid, or "unknown" when the webhook doesn't say
  skus       // the list of SKUs that were paid for
}

body.p: Everything you need is in this chapter: selectors, renaming, arithmetic, `default`, and either `map` or a selector on a list. Your script is checked against three different webhooks, so it has to follow the rules rather than the values.
When it passes, you have written a real integration mapping. Part 1 starts from here, one topic at a time.

check.prompt: Turn the payment webhook into `{ orderId, paidBy, amount, method, skus }`.
check.solution:
%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
  orderId: payload.data.orderRef,
  paidBy: payload.data.payer.name,
  amount: payload.data.amountCents / 100,
  method: payload.data.method default "unknown",
  skus: payload.data.items.sku
}
mustFail:

output application/json
---
{
  orderId: payload.data.orderRef,
  paidBy: payload.data.payer.name,

  skus: payload.data.items.sku
}

%dw 2.0
output application/json
---
{
